lead.s: Internal Medicine End of Semester CAT (MBChB 4): haematology and renal, 30 MCQs

sec.h: Microcytic anaemia (small cells, usually MCV <80 fL)
b: Thalassaemia (inherited reduced production of globin chains).
A very low MCV with a relatively preserved red-cell count can suggest thalassaemia trait; raised RDW can support iron deficiency. These are clues, not definitive diagnostic tests.

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with fatigue, brittle spoon-shaped nails, and a microcytic anaemia with an MCV below 70 fL. Which primary pathophysiological mechanism underlies this specific presentation?
o: Acute blood loss from major trauma
Decreased production due to iron deficiency
qs.e: Koilonychia and microcytic anaemia point directly toward iron deficiency causing decreased red cell production. Thalassaemias also cause microcytosis, but spoon nails are characteristic of iron shortage.
qs.s: Year 3: Haematology and Blood Transfusion Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops a microcytic anaemia. Laboratory investigations reveal a low serum iron level, low total iron-binding capacity, and a normal or high serum ferritin level. What is the primary mechanism responsible for these findings?
o: Primary stem cell dysplasia leading to ineffective erythropoiesis and ring sideroblasts
Autoimmune destruction of circulating erythrocytes by pathogenic anti-D antibodies
Absolute depletion of total body iron stores due to chronic gastrointestinal blood loss
Increased hepcidin release trapping iron in macrophages and reducing gut absorption
qs.e: Chronic inflammation in conditions like rheumatoid arthritis stimulates hepcidin release from the liver, which traps iron in macrophages and reduces gut iron absorption, causing anaemia of chronic disease with normal or high ferritin stores. This differs from true iron deficiency anaemia, where body iron stores and serum ferritin are low.
qs.s: Haematology & Blood Transfusion Pathology: MDS, Stem Cell Transplant: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis develops a microcytic anaemia. Laboratory evaluation reveals a normal to high ferritin level. What is the underlying mechanism causing this functional iron deficiency?
o: Marrow aplasia secondary to long-standing immunosuppressive drug therapy
Primary nutritional folate deficiency from systemic inflammatory cachexia
Chronic inflammation inducing hepatic hepcidin release to trap iron in macrophages
Autoimmune antibodies directly destroying circulating mature erythrocytes
qs.e: Chronic inflammation leads to hepcidin release from the liver, which traps iron in macrophages and reduces gut absorption, causing functional iron deficiency despite normal or high iron stores. Ferritin is high because it also acts as an acute-phase protein.
qs.s: Haematology & Blood Transfusion Pathology: MDS, Stem Cell Transplant: MCQs
